paragraphs: Many songbirds learn their songs from adult tutors, and populations separated by a few kilometers often sing distinct local dialects. One long-standing hypothesis holds that dialects help females recognize males of their own population and so keep locally adapted traits intact. Experiments, however, have produced mixed results: in some species, females prefer local songs, while in others, they show no preference. A second possibility, which I find at least as likely, is that dialects are merely a by-product of imperfect copying, with small errors accumulating in isolated groups much as accents do in human communities. This view predicts that dialects should differ most between groups that rarely exchange young birds, a pattern that has been reported but not yet systematically tested.
